en: Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.1: Now, therefore, one who is about to establish the sacred fire (agni) should sprinkle a mound sloping toward the northeast and make a mark in its center.

Having drawn a line toward the east and one toward the north, and having subsequently sprinkled with water the three lines in the middle facing east, he should establish the fire with the words "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ"; this is the rule for the ritual enclosure everywhere. Now, therefore, we shall explain the *pākayajñas*: the *huta*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*.

Among these, the offering (*homa*) is performed in a single fire; the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the sipping of water (*udakācamana*) are constant; and they follow either the procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-tantra*) or the procedure of the *snāna* (initiation).

Or he places a full vessel to the south of the fire, and a *sruva* ladle filled with water to the north of the fire. Having sprinkled it with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle thee," the prepared sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) become ready. He sprinkles it once with the *yajus* formula and twice silently. The fuel-stick (*idhma*) is made of *khadira* or *palāśa*; in their absence, [it may be] from any tree except for the *vibhītaka*, *tilvaka*, *bādhaka*, *nimba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *śalmali*, *aralu*, *dadhittha*, *kovidāra*, and *śleṣmātaka*.

For all forest trees, *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) consists of all grasses—excluding *śūkātṛṇa*, *śara*, *śīrya*, *balbaja*, *mutava*, *nal̤a*, and *śuṇṭha*—if *kuśa* grass is unavailable; or white *sumanas* flowers, or, in their absence, fragrant flowers of any color, excluding *japā*, *aruṣka*, *ākuttha*, *bhaṇḍī*, and *kuraṇḍaka*. There are four types of base materials for the clarified butter (*ājya*): milk from a cow with a calf, or from another animal, or simply milk. After [the oblation], there is the sipping of water (*ācamana*) behind the fire.
He should sip water three times, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the organs] while moving his hand. Having sprinkled his feet and head, he should touch the vital breaths in the head.
After touching water, he should sit down behind the fire that has been kindled and, grasping the earth with his right hand, mutter: "We partake of this of the earth;
this is auspicious and most fortunate. Drive away those who revile us; find wealth for others"—ending with the word *vasu*.

If it is night, he should sweep around the fire with this three-verse hymn of praise, or else, having thrice grasped the prastara-bunch with the first verse, he strews the grass around it in each direction, beginning from the south-east, covering the roots with the tips; or, having spread it out from the west, he should place two rows of ulapa-grass at the junction of the southern and northern sides.
JaimGS 1.2:
From the *prastara* he takes two *pavitra* strainers, each a span (*prādeśa*) long, equal in size, with unbroken tips, and without an inner core.

Holding them with his thumb and ring finger, he cuts them with his nail using the formula, "You two are *pavitra*s belonging to Viṣṇu. He should then stroke them three times upward with water while meditating on Viṣṇu in his mind.

With the formula, "You two are pure," he places the two strainers once with the *yajus* and twice silently upon the vessel. Holding them over the vessel, he pours the clarified butter (*ājya*) into it. Having drawn out embers to the north of the fire, he places the vessel over them, illuminates its contents, throws in two young *darbha* blades, carries fire around it three times, and removes it to the north.

Having pushed back the embers and holding the two strainers with their tips pointing north, he purifies the clarified butter, the sacrificial oblation, the *praṇītā* waters, and the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) three times with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless [strainer]."

With the formulas "By the purifier of Vasu," "By the rays of the sun," and "The god for you," he pours forth the *praṇītā* waters; having poured the clarified butter back once with the *yajus* formula and twice silently, and having led the *praṇītā* waters to the north of the fire, covered them with *darbha* grass, and placed the *prastara* bundle to the south of the fire, he places the two *pavitra* strainers upon the *prastara* and mutters the *virūpākṣa* mantra: "Om! Penance and truth are the self."
And steadfastness, and righteousness, and truth, and renunciation, and the Brahman, and the Brahman—those I take refuge in;
may they protect me. Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ! I ascend the Great Self. You are Virūpākṣa, the tooth-gnasher;
your bed is on a leaf, your home is in the intermediate space, and your golden dwelling is measured out there. In an iron jar, the hearts of the gods are contained.

Those [powers] are contained within; they are Balabhu, Baladha, and Rakshana. Do not be heedless! Truly, you have twelve sons who, year after year, having caused you to sacrifice with the Kāmapra sacrifice, enter again upon the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*).
You are the Brahmin among the gods, and I am the Brahmin among men. Indeed, a Brahmin seeks refuge with a Brahmin; therefore, I seek refuge with you.
"Do not murmur after me as I murmur; do not offer oblations after me as I offer oblations; do not act against me as I act. I take refuge in you;

impelled by you, I shall perform this rite. May it be successful for me! Homage to Virūpākṣa, the conqueror of teeth, the eldest son of Brahmā, the most excellent, the unfailing lord of rites. Thus [he says]. JaimGS 1.2.

Having sprinkled water on the five layers and purified them, he should offer oblations. He lays them around: the thickest one in the middle, the longest at the back, the middle-sized one to the south, and the smallest to the north. Touching each other, he pours out a vessel of water to the south of the fire with the formula, "O Aditi, give your consent!"; to the west with, "O Anumati, give your consent!"; and to the north with, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent!"

Saying, "O God Savitṛ, impel," he should sprinkle water around the fire three times, keeping his right side toward it, with the formula: "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for prosperity. May the divine Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention; may the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet. He does this once with the *yajus* formula and twice silently. Then, having taken the fuel-stick (*idhma*) and having taken clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva*-ladle and poured it over [the stick], he places it into the fire with the verse beginning "This... (RV 3.29.10).
"This fuel is your self, O Jātavedas; by it grow and increase. And you, Indra, make us grow; prosper us with offspring, cattle, spiritual luster, and the eating of food—Svāhā!

With this, he mentally offers the two Āghāra libations continuously along the diagonal. Having drawn the *sruva* spoon across the northern junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the formula "To Prajāpati, Svāhā," and having drawn it across the southern junction of the enclosing sticks with the formula "To Indra, Svāhā," he performs the two Āghāra libations.

Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers with "To Agni, svāhā! on the north, and with "To Soma, svāhā! on the south; between these two [fires] is the world of oblations.

Then he offers with "Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā! at the full moon sacrifice, and with "To Agni" and "To Agni and Soma"; at the new moon sacrifice, with "To Agni" and "To Indra and Agni," he offers the northernmost and easternmost oblation.

He offers oblation after oblation, not offering back [the spoon], from the place of the *sauviṣṭakṛt* offering toward the west; the permanent fire is in front, with the *sviṣṭakṛt* at the end, except for the offerings of the omentum and the clarified butter. He does not pour clarified butter over the *sviṣṭakṛt*. In the *sruva* spoon, he spreads a base of clarified butter once, cuts off two portions from the sacrificial food, and having poured clarified butter twice—once and again—he pours it over them, using the thumb and the fingers.

He cuts portions twice from the two pieces of flesh and twice from the sacrificial butter; having sprinkled [the portions] twice with butter, he sprinkles them back again. That is the fivefold cutting for the descendants of Jamadagni; it is done with a finger or with a tuft of grass, and this is the procedure for the oblation everywhere.

He takes up the *prastara* together with the *pavitra*. He anoints its tips in the *sruva* ladle with [the formula], "Be anointed for heaven"; the middle part in the clarified butter with, "Be anointed for the intermediate region";

and the roots in the oblation with, "Be anointed for earth. He throws a blade of grass from the *prastara* away with, "For life, thee! He then casts the *prastara* into the fire for Agni with [the formula], "To Agni, thee!"
With "To Anumati, svāhā! he throws a blade of grass after [the fire] from the west, saying, "Name my enemy; burn him up, svāhā!
He places fuel-sticks smeared with ghee for the sake of prosperity, saying, "To success, svāhā! Having touched the ground, he should touch the vital breaths in his head, saying, "To intention, svāhā!
After touching water, he offers twelve expiatory oblations: "To intention, svāhā!"... [and so on].
To desire, svāhā!
Hail to prosperity!
Accomplish the hymn with the *ṛc*; [accomplish] the *rathantara* with the *gāyatra*; [accomplish] the *bṛhat* on the path of the *gāyatra*. Svāhā!
The rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, the Sun, for all to behold; Svāhā!
The brilliant host of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Sūrya has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-air; he is the soul of all that moves and stands. Svāhā!
Rising up from out of the darkness, beholding the higher light, the heaven, we have gone to Sūrya, the god among gods, the highest light; Svāhā!
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
With whatever desire we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches. Svāhā!
Bhūḥ svāhā!
Bhuvaḥ svāhā!
Svaha! To heaven, svāhā!

Having recited "Bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," he then brings the spread darbha grass and places it over the *praṇītā* water and the *sruva* ladle; while pouring out water, he mutters: "Thou art a seat; mayest thou be my seat. Thou art all; mayest thou be all for me. Thou art full; mayest thou be full for me. Thou art imperishable; mayest thou not perish for me. He sprinkles water toward each direction, saying: "In the eastern direction, may the gods and the officiating priests purify themselves."

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he says, "May the months and the ancestors purify themselves" in the southern direction; then, becoming one who wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and touching water, he says, "May the houses and cattle purify themselves" in the western direction; "May the waters, herbs, and trees purify themselves" in the northern direction; "May the sacrifice, the year, and the lord of the sacrifice purify themselves" in the upward direction; and finally, having poured out the water with the words, "I send you forth to the ocean."

"I send you to the ocean, O unobserved ones; go back to your own source. May our heroes be unharmed; let not our own property be poured away. With these words, "O Sarasvatī, that [essence] of yours which is in the waters," he should wipe his eyes with the thumb and the ring finger. [And likewise: "O Sarasvatī, that honey of yours which is in the waters, in the cows, and in the horses..."

Having placed darbha grass and enclosing sticks into the fire with the verse, "May Sarasvatī, rich in horses, moisten my mouth," and having performed the rite of pacification (*śānti*) with the *Vāmadevya* hymn, he should sprinkle water around the fire three times while holding the sacrificial oblation. He should adapt the mantras to "thou hast consented" (*anvamaṃsthāḥ*) and "thou hast impelled" (*prāsāvīḥ*). A full vessel placed nearby is the sacrificial fee (*dakṹṣiṇā*);

JaimGS 1.5: In the third month [of pregnancy], one performs the *puṃsavana* rite—except for a cow that has calved only once (*gṛṣṭi*). Having cooked a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in clarified butter, or having prepared *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter) according to the procedure for a *sthālīpāka*, he should offer it with the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having made two beans and a barley grain into male forms, he should have her eat them with a drop of curd, saying: "Prajāpati... [and so forth].
"Puruṣa Parameṣṭhin, may he grant me a son who is long-lived and glorious; may I, with my husband, be a mother of living sons.
Having tied a shoot of the *nyagrodha* tree together with two fruits using two white threads, she should wear it around her neck. This is called the "Dhruva-kumāra" rite;
a garment is the sacrificial fee.
JaimGS 1.6:

Now, therefore, we shall explain [the rite] for the ancestors with joyful faces (*nāndīmukha-pitṛ*). During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having prepared the food on the day before—or on the very day itself, saying "I shall perform it tomorrow"—he invites pure Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas.
Being pure, having dressed in a clean, unwashed white garment, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, and having sipped water, he offers four "white" oblations—

curd, rice grains, fragrant white flowers, and *sumanas* flowers— after spreading *darbha* grass with tips pointing eastward upon the fire-altar, saying: "Homage to Agni, Soma, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, the Ṛṣis, the Bhūtas, the Pitṛs, and to all deities," and [offers] sacrificial food.

Having given [offerings] to the Brahmins with curd, black gram, fish, meat, and various foods— this is another method— then, taking four items, namely rice, barley, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds, and taking a water-pot together with those very items, one should compose the mind and say, "May you be gracious," and then, with the *praṇava*, say, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased"; thus for the others according to the purpose.
They should respond.
Jaiminīya Gṛhya Sūtra 1.7:

One should perform the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) in the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, during the bright fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion or under the asterisms of Hasta or the Uttarās.
Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* mixed with sesame and mung beans, he should offer it while [the wife] maintains contact; having offered the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he should proceed.

Then, having seated her on an auspicious seat behind the fire, or on a white woolen cloth spread over a higher surface, he should make a parting of her hair with a porcupine quill having three white spots, reaching as far as the breaths, from the front toward the crown of the head, saying: "For out-breathing thee! For in-breathing thee!
Then, having adorned her right hair-parting with garlands, and likewise the left, he [places] a bronze vessel of water containing gold.

Having filled it, he should look at her there and ask, "O Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, what do you see? She replies, "Offspring, cattle, good fortune, and long life for my husband. A garment or gold is the sacrificial fee. JaimGS_1.7 //
Jaimini Gṛhya Sūtra 1.8:
When a son is born, the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) is performed before the first feeding with breast milk. Having rubbed rice and barley together with gold, he should feed [the child] while reciting:
"This is food; this is sap; this is immortality along with breath. The earth is your mother, the sky is your father; live!"
"May you see a hundred autumns; may you see a hundred autumns," he says. Then he addresses him with the mantra: "From limb by limb you arise, from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self (ātman) named son; live for a hundred autumns, may you see a hundred autumns. Then he entrusts him [to the day]: "To the day..."

"I entrust you to the day; may the day entrust you to the night; may the night entrust you to day and night; may day and night entrust you to the half-months; may the half-months entrust you to the months; may the months entrust you to the seasons; may the seasons entrust you to the year; may the year entrust you to old age and death. "Who are you? Which one are you?"

"Be cool," he says; "Enter me, so-and-so," he says; then he gives him a secret name, saying, "You are the Veda. Then he smells his head, saying, "Become a stone, become an axe, become unconquerable gold; with the *hiṃkāra* of cattle, I smell you.
In this very same way, upon returning from a journey abroad, he smells the heads of his sons. For ten nights, he [offers] mustard seeds mixed with chaff into the fire.
One should offer oblations with these two verses: "To Śaṇḍa and Marka, to Upavīra, to Śauṇḍikera, to Ulūkhala, to Malimluca, to Duṇāśin, and to Cyavana—let them perish from here, svāhā!
Ālikhat, Vilikhant, Animiṣan, Kiṃvadanta, Upaśruti, Aryamaṇa, Kumbhī, Śatru, Pātrapāṇi, and Nipuṇahāntrīmukha."

"May the one who is as harsh as mustard seed perish from here, svāhā!"—for ten nights the husband and wife are in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka); at the end of that period, they rise after bathing.
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.9:

Now, therefore, follows the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*). On the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on the twelfth day, the father—or the teacher, or the father acting as the teacher—should give him a name.
Having wrapped him all around with a new garment, the father should sit with him on his own lap; this is his naming.

One should give [a name] consisting of two syllables or four syllables, beginning and ending with a sonant, containing a semivowel, not corresponding to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a deity, and not formed with a secondary suffix (*taddhita*); for a woman, it should end in long *ā*, or it may be according to the actual meaning. And in the rites for boys, one sacrifices to the lunar mansion, the deity of that lunar mansion, and the lunar day (*tithi*).
He sacrifices to these eight other favored deities: Agni, Dhanvantari, Prajāpati, Indra, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Viśvedevas.
When the Sviṣṭakṛt offerings have been performed, all the deities become propitiated.

JaimGS 1.10: Now, therefore, follows the rite of the first feeding. During the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having fed the Brahmins, he should have [the child] eat sacrificial food with the mantra: "O Lord of Food, grant us food that is free from disease and full of vigor.
Further the giver; bestow strength upon us, and welfare upon our two-footed and four-footed creatures. JaimGS 1.10.
JaimGS 1.11:

In the third year [of conception], he should let his hair grow matted; according to some, when the child has reached the third year. During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having had the Brahmins pronounce blessings, and having carried forward the fire in the afternoon, he places four full vessels to the south of the fire.

He should place grains of rice and barley on both sides, with sesame and beans in the middle. When the student has sipped water and is holding on [to the teacher], he should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;

having offered these, he offers the fifth oblation here with the Virūpākṣa formula. They bring forth warm water with all the herbs—rice, barley, sesame, and beans—this constitutes "all the herbs. He takes up the razor with the verse: "Savitar has come hither with the razor, authorized by all the gods and the Maruts."
"May Viśvakarman be auspicious to us; do you all protect us always with blessings. With the words, "Come hither, O Vāyu, with warm water," he takes up water.

With the words, "Come hither, O Vāyu, with warm water; may Aditi shave the hair," and "May the waters moisten [it] for life," he moistens the right side of the hair. With the words, "May the waters moisten [it] for life, for long-lasting vitality and luster," he places three blades of *darbha* grass upon that [hair], or one.

"Or let Prajāpati hold [the razor]," he should say; "let Prajāpati hold it again and again, O excellent shaver," having thus touched [the hair] three times upward with a mirror, he should cut it with the razor [reciting]: "With that by which Dhātṛ shaved for the sake of the life of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra—with that I shave you for the sake of life, for good renown, and for well-being. "With that by which Prajāpati shaved for the Maruts, the householders... [he should recite].

"With that [blade] I shave you for long life, for good renown, and for well-being"—with this mantra, he shaves him on the front side; "with that [blade] I shave you for long life, for good renown, and for well-being"—in this same way, he shaves him on the back and likewise on the north side, reciting the mantra for each.

He should place the hair, the remains of the *darbha* stalks, and the clumps of hair upon the bull's dung that has not touched the ground. For a Brāhmaṇa, he places them to the east; for the other two castes, to the west. With the mantra, "Whatever [hair] the razor... (he continues).

He should hand the razor to the barber with the formula: "O barber, with that razor by which you shave the limbs of men, making them pure—do not harm my life or my luster, O barber! According to their specific family custom or clan tradition, if [the ritual] has been omitted, he should offer expiatory oblations; for a woman, he should perform it according to the same procedure but without mantras. If it was performed with mantras, he should offer five oblations, and then, beginning from his head, he mutters [the following].

"May there be the triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Jamadagni, and that triple life-span which belongs to the gods—may that triple life-span be yours. With these words, the performer of the rite for well-being should bury the hair in a grain-pool or a cow-pen; he should carry away full vessels, and a cow is the sacrificial fee.
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.12:

One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the seventh year, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in the fifth, and one desiring long life in the ninth; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth.
One should not initiate [any of them] beyond the sixteenth year, for he has then shed his virility and becomes a *vṛṣala*.

Then they bring him, having bathed, adorned, anointed his eyes, and had the barber’s work performed upon him; he should clothe him with a new garment with the verse, according to the respective caste: "We clothe this Soma with the sacred word (*brahman*) for great hearing, so that old age may reach him, and that he may long remain awake in his hearing; may he live a hundred autumns, may he see a hundred autumns. [And with the verse: "We clothe this Indra with the sacred word for great sovereignty..."

"May old age come to him; may he watch over the house for a long time. Live a hundred autumns; see a hundred autumns"—thus [he says]. "O Brāhmaṇas, we place this one in prosperity for great prosperity.
May old age come to him; may he watch over prosperity for a long time. Live a hundred autumns; see a hundred autumns.

Then, having seated him behind the fire facing east and wearing the sacrificial cord (yajñopavīta), the teacher makes him sip water; once he has sipped, he makes him rise and [seats him] to the north.

Having spread eastward-pointed darbha grass in front of the fire and having placed an unbroken stone upon it, he should make him step upon that stone with his right foot, saying: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm; drive away the hater, and let not the hater strike thee. Then, having seated him behind the fire facing eastward, the teacher stands to the north, while the student maintains contact with him.

One should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and with Vedic oblations; having poured the remnants into his mouth, one should cause him—who has eaten and sipped water—to rise, and lead him clockwise around the fire while reciting for each mantra: "bhūr ṛcaḥ svāhā," "bhuvo yajūṃṣi svāhā," and "svaḥ sāmāni svāhā. Then, saying "namo vātāya," he should lead him around the fire, [reciting]: "Homage to Vāta! Homage be to Agni! Homage to Pṛthivī!"

"Obeisance to the plants; obeisance to you, the unseen and great one, I pay it"—with these words, the student should approach, saying, "O giver, bestow this Veda upon such-and-such a person. Then, having stationed him behind the fire facing eastward, the teacher stands before him facing westward; they both form water-pots. The teacher stands to the north; another should fill his pot with water, while the filling of the other's is done by means of the overflow. Then he instructs him.
"I have come to the life of sacred study (*brahmacarya*); lead me near. "Who are you by name? "I am so-and-so," he should give his name. Thereupon the teacher mutters:
"Hiṃ! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We have come together; may you keep the mortal far away.
May we move about unharmed; may this one walk in well-being. Then, with his own right hand, [he takes] his right hand.
"Indra has taken your hand; Dhātṛ has taken your hand; Pūṣan has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand; Yama has taken your hand; you are Mitra by law;
Agni is your teacher"—with these words he takes his hand. Then, beginning from the region of the navel, he mutters: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen.
Having touched the right shoulder with the words, "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; do not loosen; make an interval between death and immortality," he touches it.
"May [the vow] be in me; let your heart be mine; let your mind follow my mind. Accept my word with single-minded devotion. May Bṛhaspati unite you with me. Then he entrusts him [to the guardians]:
"I entrust you to Agni; I entrust you to Vāyu; I entrust you to Dyau (Heaven) and Savitṛ; I entrust you to the Waters and the Plants."

"I entrust you to all the gods; I entrust you to all beings; I entrust you for safety. Then he instructs him: "You are a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*); place fuel on the fire; drink water; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day. [The student says: "I have brought fuel for Agni.
Thus, with fuel-sticks anointed with ghee, he places them on the fire, saying: "I have brought fuel for Agni, the great Jātavedas."
Just as you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel, so may I prosper with long life, luster, brilliance, gain, wisdom, insight, offspring, cattle, Vedic splendor, food, and wealth— svāhā!
The wisdom that is among the Apsarases, and the mind that is among the Gandharvas—may that divine wisdom, born of man, the fragrant wisdom, attend me; Svāhā!

"Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā! With these words, she should fasten the girdle, saying: "May this goddess, this auspicious girdle, come to me—driving away what is ill-spoken, warding off what is ill-done, purifying my pure color, and bringing strength through the out-breath and in-breath."
"Guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the far-reaching protector of ascetic heat (*tapas*), striking down the *rakṣas* and overcoming the malevolent ones—come to me from all sides, O auspicious one!

O girdle (*mekhalā*), may your wearer not come to harm! With these words, he girds him with a girdle of *muñja* grass for a Brāhmaṇa, one of bowstring (*maurvī*) for a Rājanya, or one of *tāmalī* wood mixed with *muñja* for a Vaiśya; or else a *muñja* girdle for all. Then follow the garments.

The inner garment of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of linen or hemp; the upper garment should be made of deer-skin: that of a Rājanya from the skin of the *raurava* deer, and that of a Vaiśya from goat-skin; or, according to some, all may wear the *eṇeya* deer-skin.

He should hand over the staff with the formula, "Thou art the promoter of well-being. It should reach up to his mouth; for a Brāhmaṇa it is of *pālāśa* wood, for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) it is of *bilva* wood, for a Rājanya it is of *naiyagrodha* wood, and for a Vaiśya it is of *audumbara* wood; or, alternatively, it may be of *pālāśa* wood for all.

One should first beg from the mother of all [the women present], and then from other female friends. A Brāhmaṇa should beg using the form beginning with "bhavatī": "Bhavati, give me alms. A Rājanya should beg using the form with "bhavat" in the middle: "Bhavati, give alms. A Vaiśya should beg using the form with "bhavat" at the end:
"Dehi bhikṣāṃ bhavatī. One should not increase the syllables *kṣāṃ* and *hiṃ*; or rather, all should use the form beginning with "bhavat," for which there is an expiation.

If [the student] should revive, [the teacher] should say, "O living ones, give life to me," and he should have him sip water with [the formula]: "O living ones, give life to me; you are waters by name, you are immortals by name, you are *svadhā* by name; may I enjoy you; place me in your good-will; be auspicious to me; homage be to you; do not harm me. When alms have been brought after three nights have passed, [he should teach] the *Sāvitrī*.

Or he may recite it on that very day; afterwards, having recited the entire [Veda] verse by quarter, half-verse, and whole verse, and having taken hold of the Veda, he places fuel-sticks smeared with ghee into the fire while reciting: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me, svāhā! O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow;
may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me, svāhā!"

"O Vāyu, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so; may it be accomplished for me, svāhā! O Āditya, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me, svāhā!
O Vratapati, Lord of Vows, I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so; may it be successful for me, svāhā! This is the instruction regarding the observance of the vow (*vrātādeśana*).

At the conclusion of every vow, he should modify the mantras by reciting: "O Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I have been able to do it; it has been accomplished for me, Svāhā! Then he instructs him: "O student, remain dependent on your teacher, be tranquil, sleep on the ground, and wear a staff, a girdle, an antelope skin, and matted hair; avoid untruth, honey, meat, perfumes, and garlands. For three nights he shall not eat pungent or salty food; after those three nights, [he should face] the east.

Or, having gone out toward the northern direction and approached a Palāśa tree, having anointed it with the Vyāhṛtis and sacrificed with a *sthālīpāka* offering, he should cast away his sacrificial cord and staff, return home, and give a cow as the sacrificial fee.
JaimGS 1.13:

In the evening and in the morning, having become pure at the water's edge and being equipped with a strainer (*pavitra*), one should purify oneself with water using the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *taratsamandī dhāvati*, and the *vāmadevya* hymn at the end; sitting on *darbha* grass in a clean place, holding *darbha* grass in one's hand.

Facing westward and restraining his speech, he should meditate on the twilight with his mind until the rising of the stars. When the stars have risen, having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he should recite the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times or one hundred times, or at least ten times. Then he worships Agni with the verse, "O Agni, you are our nearest [kinsman]. Then he worships Varuṇa with the verse, "You, O Varuṇa, and also Mitra," following the same procedure.

In the morning, standing facing the east, he then worships the sun with the verse, "Up from the darkness" (RV 7.89.2). Then he worships Mitra with the verse, "To Mitra, to Aryaman" (RV 10.87.1). If he has been overtaken by sunrise or sunset, he should mentally meditate on the remainder of the Sāvitrī; that itself is the expiation in that case.
JaimGS 1.14:

On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with the *hasta* [mantra] and having sipped water (ācamana), they all recite the following prayer at the beginning:
"May there be union for us; may it nourish us together; may our vigor be united; may we not be at variance with one another. For all [of them].
He should recite the Sāvitrī to them with the words, "May you be endowed with vigor," just as at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Having mentally recited the *Sāmasāvitrī* and the verses beginning with "Soma the King," and having studied the Vedic meters (*chandas*) according to their purpose, he offers nine oblations of unbroken grains (*akṣatadhānā*) and curd, [addressing] the Ṛṣis, the meters, the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the straight path, and the Sāman: "We worship the Lord of the Assembly (*sadasaspati*), the wonderful one..."

With the verse beginning "medhākāram," he should first satisfy the teacher with the six preceding [verses], and then [the following]: Jaimini, Talavakāra, Sātyamugra, Rāṇāyani, Durvāsas, Bhāguri, Gauruṇiḍa, Gaurgulavi, the venerable Aupamanyava,
Kāraḍi, Sāvarṇi, Gārgya, Vārṣagaṇya, and Daivantya— these thirteen— with [the verses] containing the word *dhānā* and the verse addressed to Dadhikrāvan.

Having consecrated the remainder of the oblation with these two [verses] and having consumed it, the [sacrificial animal] is assigned during the forenoon: a goat when the Āgneya section is completed, a ram for the Aindra, and a cow for the Pāvamāna; this is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the Parvan. He should feed his fellow students who have gathered there. Regarding the day of the Sāvitra ceremony and the Utsarga, he should not eat meat for three nights, nor should he perform a Śrāddha, nor have his hair shaved, nor approach his wife even during her season.
One may approach one's wife during the rainy season and autumn; some say for half a month.
JaimGS 1.15:

In the month of Taiṣya, there is the suspension of Vedic study. Having performed the dismissal with the formula, "May the Vedas rest according to their own [nature]; may the meters, increasing by four syllables each, contemplate us with auspiciousness," they should suspend both teaching and studying.
While observing their vows, they should study their respective Vedas; from that time onward, they do not study during the rainy months (*abhra*).

The Gaudānika, Vrātika, and Aupaniṣada vows last for one year each. During these, there is the ritual touching of water (ablution) in the evening and in the morning; one must not eat without having touched water.
Having touched water in the morning and evening, the Vrātika of the Āditya [vow] should fetch a fuel-stick from the forest and place it on the fire before the offering of the firewood.

For one year he should wear a single garment; he should not mount the sun [by looking directly at it], nor should he cover himself with a parasol while on the earth. He should not swim across water above the knees, except by the command of his teacher. During the Vrataparvan of the Ādityavrātika, he should cause him to hear the Śukriyas, the Upaniṣads, and the Upaniṣadic texts. Jaimini Gṛhya Sūtra 1.16.
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.17:

There are alternative options for twelve *mahānāmnikā* years—namely nine, six, or three; some say it is one year. If the *mahānāmnyas* have been heard from his father, he should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year, wearing a single white garment; however, he should remain standing during the day for the greater part of the vow, and sit at other times.

Some say that his food and clothing at night should be black; however, he should wear only white, for he should not wear black due to the fault of passion. He should touch water in all circumstances, thinking, "The *śakvarī* verses have been recited. He should not bathe in a boat, unless there is a danger to life, in which case he may touch water. Or rather, he should cause cows to drink [the water], thinking, "The *śakvarī* verses have been recited. He should not let rain fall upon him, but should hold up a parasol against the rain.

As he performs this [rite], Parjanya rains according to his desire. At the conclusion of his studentship (*brahmacarya*), having fasted for one night and gone to the forest, he should fill a bronze vessel with water mixed with *śaivala* moss. Having seated him there and surrounded him on all sides, while he keeps his eyes closed, the teacher should chant three *stotriya* verses. Then, rising, the teacher should wrap the student's face with an unwashed garment, and [place] a vessel of water to the right.

He should remain holding [the vessel] for the remainder of the day, or sit through the night with his speech restrained. On the following morning, having gone to the forest, kindled the fire, and brought a calf near, he should unwrap his garment, lift up a bronze vessel, and look at the water, saying, "Look at the sun! He should look at the sun, saying, "Look at the light! He should look at the fire, saying, "Look at the light! He should look at the calf, saying, "Look at the animal! He should look at the water with the verse, "Coming together... (RV 10.9.4).

Having poured out the garment, the bronze vessel, and the calf with the verse "vatsam," he should present them to the teacher; from the *sthalīpāka* [he should offer] to Viśvāmitra and Indra, and to the Mahānāmnīs;
he should feed the teacher together with his retinue, and a cow is the sacrificial fee.

Jaimini-Gṛhya-Sūtra 1.18: Some say that the Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*) lasts twelve years from birth, or as long as the study [of the Veda] takes; always the placing of fuel on the fire in the evening, and the begging of alms in the evening and morning; one should avoid two *trivṛt* [verses], and the *trivṛt* amulet [should be avoided] when it is threefold.

In the sixteenth year, there is the performance of the *godāna* ceremony; they call that the *keśānta* ceremony. The mantras are explained by those used for the *caula* ceremony. The instruction regarding the vows follows that of the *upanayana*, but here [the following differences apply]: the garment is not prescribed as being new or unwashed; one should have all the hair and nails shaved, except for the topknot (*śikhā*). According to Audgāhamani, one should bathe with the hair left unshorn, using the "of the tree" (*vanaspate*) formula, which refers to the bathing substance derived from trees.

He rubs the skin [off his body] with the formula: "Thou art the skin of the tree; thou art purifying; purify me. He applies that [ointment] to himself with the formula: "I take thee for long life and splendor. Having bathed, he applies ointment with the formula: "Thou art the fragrance of the trees. [He says: "Thou art the fragrance of the trees, of holy scent; grant me a holy scent among gods and men. I take thee for long life and splendor."

With the words, "For splendor," he ties on a garland of flowers from trees with the formula: "Thou art the flower of trees; O thou of holy fragrance, make my fragrance holy among gods and men! I offer thee for long life and splendor. With the words, "Thou art a mirror," he should look at himself in a mirror: "Thou art a mirror; may both gods and men see me! Thou art beauty; may I attain beauty!"

"Among gods and men you are the radiant one; may I be radiant among gods and men"—having thus removed the garland, he should cause [the student] to be instructed. The rules have been stated; in the case of the annual sacrifices, a cow is the sacrificial fee.

Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.19: Having studied the Veda and performed the vows, a Brāhmaṇa, intending to bathe [the initiation bath], prepares the necessary materials: an unwashed garment, a grass mat, [materials for] bathing, ointment, flowers, collyrium, a mirror, two new garments, a three-stranded amulet, and a bamboo staff.

The barber, having prepared two white sandals, stands to the north. Having spread out *erakā* grass and covered [the boy] with a new garment whose fringes point northward, he seats him there facing east and should plunge the staff into the water with the mantra, "Thou art the thunderbolt of the hater.

He should loosen the girdle with the mantra, "Upwards the highest," and he should likewise plunge that too into the water; the mantras for the cutting of the hair-ends have been explained; this is the shaving.

And he shaves the head first, then the beard, then the other limbs in due order; he should bury the hair, beard, body-hair, and nails at the root of an Aśvattha tree or an Udumbara tree with the mantra, "May my sin be struck away. He should bathe him with cold and warm water over which gold has been placed, with the mantra, "Be auspicious to us, most peaceful, O Sarasvatī, full of joy; may your open space not be seen by us," under the Rohiṇī asterism.

One should bathe under Mṛgaśiras, thinking, "This is the constellation of Prajāpati; may I become possessed of offspring. One should bathe under Tiṣya, thinking, "This is the constellation of Soma; may the sacrifice to Soma come to me. One should bathe under Hasta, thinking, "This is the constellation of Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is the sacred word (brahman); may I become endowed with the splendor of the sacred word. One should bathe under Anūrādhās, thinking, "This is the constellation of Savitṛ; may I be impelled by Savitṛ."
One should bathe under the asterism of Maitra, thinking, "May I become dear to friends. One should bathe under Śravaṇa, for this is the asterism of Viṣṇu;

Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, [thinking], "May the sacrifice come to me. He should clothe himself with a new garment, saying, "Around this Soma... First, he should apply collyrium to his left eye, saying, "May I be glorious," and then to his right. He then fastens a three-stranded amulet around his neck.

One desiring well-being should take up a staff of *pālāśa* wood with the formula, "Thou art well-being"; one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should take up a staff of *bailva* wood with the formula, "May I become possessed of spiritual luster"; one desiring food should take up a staff of *ārka* wood with the formula, "May I become possessed of food, an eater of food"; and he should take up a bamboo staff with the formula, "Thou art the Gandharva Viśvāvasu;
protect me, guard me," and he should put on sandals with the formula, "Ye are the two leaders; lead me."
Saying "Me," he first fastens [the girdle] around his right side. His vows are as follows: he should not seek jesting with one whose hair has not yet grown;
when it rains, he should not run; he should not carry his sandals himself; he should not gather fruit himself; he should not go to another village in the evening;
he should not travel alone; he should not be with *vṛṣalas*; he should not look into a well; he should not climb a tree; he should not climb a bridge; and he should not sit without a covering.

One should not eat food that has been brought in through a door other than the main entrance; nor should one eat what is sour, twice-cooked, or stale—except for vegetables, meat, barley-meal, flour-cakes, parched grain, molasses, curd, honey, and ghee. One should not laugh without covering the mouth, nor bathe naked, nor utter indecent words.
One should avoid gossip about people and quarrels. "There are three kinds of *snātakas*," so said Āruṇi Gautama.

There are three types of graduates: the graduate by knowledge (*vidyā-snātaka*), the graduate by vows (*vrata-snātaka*), and the graduate by both knowledge and vows (*vidyā-vrata-snātaka*). Among these, the last is the most excellent; the first two are equal.

Having bathed, he should say to his teacher, "May your honor bring me the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)," or he may follow the procedure for the teacher himself. To him, as he sits facing east, he should offer the honey-mixture—consisting of the seat (*viṣṭara*), water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*)—one by one in due order. He sits upon the seat with the water for the feet.
He washes my feet with the formula, "May Śrī take refuge in me," first washing the left foot; if he is a Śūdra, [he uses] "May Padyā-Virāj [take refuge] in me," and then the right foot.

He should accept the *arghya* water with the formula, "May splendor (*varcas*) be in me. He should sip the *ācamanīya* water. The cup and bowl, placed upon the two bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*), have their tips joined together at the bottom;
there is one bundle of grass to the north. Between those two, curd and honey are placed.
If it is a *dadhimantha* (curd-mash) with curds, an *idamantha* (water-mash) with water, or a *payasyā* (milk-preparation) with milk, he should accept it with the formula, "Thee for the god...

Having accepted it, having placed it on the ground, and having touched it with his thumb and ring finger, he should eat it three times with the formula, "Thee for me for glory, for fortune, for the eating of food, and for sacred luster. He should then take the remainder to the north.

One should give it to a Brāhmaṇa after sprinkling it with water, or one may bury it in a pit for another. Seeing the cow, while holding an axe in his hand, he says, "Cow! Cow! and consecrates her with the mantra: "The cow is a milch-cow; Om, release her! If she is to be used, he should say, "Use her"; [if not], he should say, "The cow is a milch-cow, fit for sacrifice."
She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, and the navel of immortality.
Let me speak now to the discerning person: "Do not kill the cow, the sinless Aditi; let her drink water and eat grass.

Now, there are six who are worthy of the Arghya reception: the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), the graduate (*snātaka*), the consecrated king, a dear friend, and one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
He should offer hospitality to them with a cow; he should consecrate it with the formula, "These are for the guests."
Jaiminīya Gṛhya Sūtra 1.20:

Having bathed, he should attend upon his mother and father and remain dependent on them; authorized by them, he should take a wife who is of the same caste, not of the same *gotra*, not a *sapiṇḍa* of his mother, younger than himself, and one whose elder sister is unmarried. He addresses the messenger with the verse: "anṛkṣarā..."
"May the paths be straight, by which our friends go to choose a bride for us.

May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; may lordship over the household be well-governed, O gods. With these words, he addresses the fire as it is being brought during the taking of the hand: "May Agni come first among the deities;
may he release her offspring from the noose of death."

Therefore, let King Varuṇa grant his permission so that this woman may not weep over the sin committed against her grandson. One should stand before the blazing fire [reciting]: "May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have a living husband whose lap is never empty; may she awaken to the joy of seeing her grandson. A Brāhmaṇa [should stand] to the east of the fire.

Restraining his speech and facing westward, he should stand to the south of the fire holding a water-pot. His mother should hold a winnowing basket containing parched grains mixed with *śamī* leaves; in the absence of the mother, her sister or a female relative should do so. To the west of the fire, she should place either a reed-mat (*erakā*) or a thorny branch (*tejanī*), or something else of a similar kind, having wound it around so that, when the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is being spread, its western half reaches it. Then [she places] her two garments for her.

Having sprinkled [the garment] and consecrated it with the mantra, he gives it [to her], saying: "May those goddesses who cut, who spun, who wove, and those divine ones who gave the ends on both sides—may those goddesses clothe you with old age; put on this garment, O long-lived one! He should say to her: "Tread upon this eraka-grass with your right foot. If she does not recite the mantra, he himself should recite: "May the path by which my husband goes be prepared for me. He should throw [the grass] toward her.

Having thus seated his wife on an *erakā* grass mat to the south, the husband should sit to the north; both should hold onto each other, and he himself should offer the oblations loudly while she holds onto him.

Having offered with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, he offers with the seven verses beginning "She who lies across. He should pour the residue of the first offering upon her head with the verse: "She who lies across, settling down, saying 'I am the supporter'."
Thee, with the stream of what is held firm, we propitiate through complete success; for the sake of complete success, svāhā!
Let no cry of lamentation rise in your house at night; let those other than you who weep lie down elsewhere.
Do not, with disheveled hair, strike your breast; as one whose husband lives, shine in the world of your husband, rejoicing and beholding your offspring, Svāhā!
May Anumati today approve our sacrifice among the gods.
And may Agni, the bearer of oblations, accomplish that; may it be successful, svāhā!
May Dyaus protect your back; may Vāyu and the Aśvins protect your thighs; may Savitṛ protect your suckling sons;
may Bṛhaspati and the Viśvedevas protect you from behind until the putting on of the garment—Svāhā!
Childlessness, the death of a grandson, and even evil—having cast these off like a garland from one's head, I fasten the noose upon my enemies; svāhā!
Whatever evils have occurred in any of your limbs, may they all be extinguished by these oblations of clarified butter; svāhā!
"O Prajāpati," is one [verse]. (JaimGS 1.20)

Then, with his right hand, he takes her right hand: for a male, the palm; for a female, the fingers; for one desiring a couple, including the thumb. "I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband."
The gods have bestowed upon me for the sake of householdership this Savitṛ, the bestower of abundance and the lord of the house.
Soma gave her to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave her to Agni;
and Agni gave her to me, along with wealth and sons.
"Soma was the first to find [a wife], Gandharva found her next;

Agni is your third husband, and I, born of man, am the fourth. With these words, according to the procedure for the initiation (*upanayana*), he should cause her to step upon a stone to the north-east of the fire while she is being looked at by her wife. He then mutters: "Be one with no fierce eye, not a slayer of my husband, and be auspicious to me."
Well-disposed toward your husbands, radiant with luster, a mother of living sons, and loving the gods— be gracious to us, bringing welfare to our bipeds and welfare to our quadrupeds.
May Prajāpati generate offspring for us; may Aryaman grant us long life. Free from ill fortune, enter the world of your husband; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds.
O Pūṣan, bring her toward us who is most auspicious, she in whom men sow their seed;
she who, desiring us, shall spread her thighs apart, and in whom we, desiring her, may strike our phallus.

"I am the *am* (the syllable *a*), you are the *sā*; I am the *Sāman*, you are the *Ṛc*; I am the mind, you are speech; I am the sky, you are the earth. Come, let us two unite; let us both deposit seed for the sake of a male son who shall know [us]. Be devoted to me; be my equal bedfellow, O So-and-so!"—having thus taken her name, they should circumambulate the fire, with the verse: "Thou art *ṛt* (truth), O thou whose name is *Mātā* (Mother)."

"Come to me with offspring, with abundance of wealth! When she has returned, the brother or some other friend, having poured fried grains (*lāja*) that have been sprinkled with clarified butter from a winnowing basket into his joined palms, should offer them into the fire while making an under-layer and a pouring-over of butter, saying: "This maiden, going to the world of her husband from her fathers, has chosen this consecration (*dīkṣā*);
Svāhā!"—with the verse: "The maiden, O noble lady, [has come] to Aryaman. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.6).
This woman, scattering parched grain into the fire, addresses it:
"May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper! Svāhā!"
"The maidens have worshipped the divine Aryaman;

may that divine Aryaman release this woman from here and from me, Svāhā!"—at the end of each oblation, he mutters this. "And with thee, may we cross over all enemies as if crossing streams of water"—with this [verse], silently, he should pour out the fourth portion of the right side of the winnowing basket for his desire. For his desire.
Thus they say: to the north-east of the fire, he should cause her to step forward seven steps, with one mantra for each step: "One for food—may Viṣṇu follow thee!
"Two for strength—may Viṣṇu follow thee! "Three for the increase of wealth—may Viṣṇu follow thee!"
"May Viṣṇu follow those four [steps] for the sake of bliss;

may Viṣṇu follow those six [steps] for the sake of the seasons. Be a seven-stepped friend," he says. Having caused her to stand facing east at the seventh step, they should sprinkle her with water from a water-pot while reciting the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭha*. He addresses the onlookers: "This bride is auspicious; let her..."
"Come, look!
Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart toward the setting sun," he says, causing her to look. She gazes at the *dhruva* star and the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*), declaring, "May I see them.
He worships the *dhruva* with the formula: "Thou art firm; may I be firm in the family of my husband, O [Name]! (specifying the name of the husband).

She should utter her husband’s name, saying, “So-and-so”; and she should utter her own name, saying, “May I, by means of this [husband], become unobstructed like Arundhatī,” while pronouncing her own name as “So-and-so.”
With the verse, "May Pūṣan lead you from here," he addresses the bride as she has set out: "May Pūṣan lead you from here by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.

Go to the house so that you may be the mistress of the house; may you be a controller and speak with authority in the assembly. When she has reached her own family, those of virtuous character [welcome her].

"May your offspring be auspicious; having reached old age together, descend [from the bed]. May you be blessed with beloved children; remain watchful here for the sake of the household fire in this home.

Unite your body with this husband, and then, living long, may you attend the assembly. Having thus helped her descend, he should cause her to sit upon the hide of an ox with the hair facing upward, [reciting]: "Here let the cows sit down, here the horses, and here the men!"
With the words, "May Pūṣan, accompanied by a thousand sacrificial fees, sit down here," she should place the boy on her lap and pour in the parched grain fragments.

Having raised the boy, while he holds onto her, she should offer oblations with the eight verses ending in *svāhā*, beginning with: "Here is stability; here is self-stability; here is delight; here do thou rejoice! (i.e., *iha dhṛtir iha svadhṛtir iha rantiḥ iha ramasva*).

"May there be steadfastness in me; may there be self-steadfastness in me; may there be delight in me; may you delight in me. For three nights, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, practicing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and not turning away from one another, they should lie together. After the third night, at the time of union during the night, the husband and wife should perform the ritual actions and offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitti*). He should offer them with the mantra: "O Agni, you are the expiation of the gods; I, a Brahmin, [offer you] desiring protection."
I fly to you for refuge; that body of hers which is destructive to offspring, drive that away from her, svāhā!
O Vāyu, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, fly to you for refuge; that body of hers which is destructive to cattle, drive that away from her, svāhā!
O Sūrya, you are the expiation among the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa seeking protection, fly to you for refuge; that body of hers which is destructive to her husband, drive that away from her, svāhā!

"O Candra, you are the expiation; you are the expiation of the gods. I, desiring protection, take refuge in you, O Brahmāṇaspati. Whatever body of hers is destructive to the household, drive that away from her, Svāhā! O Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Candra, you are the expiations; you are the expiations of the gods. I, desiring protection, take refuge in you, O Brāhmaṇas. Whatever body of hers is destructive to her fame, drive that away from her, Svāhā! [With these words, he offers] from the *sthālīpāka* into the fire.
Having sacrificed to Prajāpati and poured the remnants into a cup, he should say to her, "Baste the channels! First the navel, then those that are above it, then those that are below;
before midnight she should lie down with this triplet: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. (And also: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms."
May Prajāpati sprinkle [you]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Bestow the embryo, O Sinīvālī; bestow the embryo, O Sarasvatī.
May the two divine Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, place the embryo within you.

"O Aśvins, that golden fire-drill which you two churned out—that embryo I place within you, so that you may give birth to it in the tenth month. Having offered oblations in this very manner at each seasonal period during the act of lying together, he should give a cow to the teacher; if [the teacher] is not present, he should give a cow to the Brahmins.

In the evening and in the morning, he offers the first oblation with the words, "To Agni, Svāhā! and the subsequent one with "To Prajāpati, Svāhā! In the same way in the morning, but with "Sūrya" in place of "Agni. Having increased the portions for the morning and evening meals, he offers them in the eastern fire with:
"To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To Dhanvantari, Svāhā! To Heaven and Earth, Svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, Svāhā! To all [the deities], Svāhā!"
With the formula, "To the deities, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! he offers the subsequent oblation with his mind from that very same northern side of the fire, saying:

"To those who are exhilarating, trembling, bringing prosperity, and who move along following the brilliance of the wind—to them I offer this oblation, desiring food; may there be for me abundant food rich in milk. He should do so in the place where hunger is present.

With the formula, "To Death as the presiding deity, svāhā," he performs the offering of the remainder. He carries the *bali* offering to the domestic deities with the words: "I bring this *bali* to the domestic deities; may they enjoy it; may they protect me; may they guard me; may they preserve me; homage to them; to them, svāhā! [He offers it] at the water-jar, in the middle of the house, in the northeastern part, at the bed, on the threshold, at the door-panels, and at the place of the *brahman*.
In these receptacles, one should always pour the remainder for Dhanvantari; this recitation of blessings in the houses is called the Great Peace (Mahāśānti).
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 1.24:
One who is about to sacrifice with new grain should first sacrifice with old grain to Agni, Dhanvantari, Prajāpati, and Indra; he should then perform nine oblations with new grain:
cakes of rice in autumn, of barley in spring, and of śyāmāka in the rainy season, dedicated to Indra-Agni, the Viśvedevas, and Heaven and Earth.

When the *ekacarū* has been spoken of, the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) are performed; he cuts off two portions for the oblation, and then he should eat [of it] with the mantra:

"O Gods, you have led us from ill to well-being; through you as our food, may we enjoy you. Enter us, O Food, as one who brings delight; be auspicious to our offspring and to our bodies. And: "They have ploughed this barley, mixed with honey, upon the Sarasvatī, according to the mind."

"Indra was the lord of the plough, the performer of a hundred rites; the Maruts were the liberal givers of the ploughmen"—with these words he should eat of barley. "May Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is;
may he make the plants auspicious for us, O Lord of all people"—with these words he should eat of *śyāmāka* grain; he should eat. (JaimGS 1.24)
Thus ends the preceding Jaimini-sūtra.
Jaiminīya Gṛhya Sūtra 2.1:

Those intending to perform a *śrāddha* shall bathe, put on clean garments, scatter sesame seeds over the site, and while performing the ritual with the left hand, they should prepare the food. Having sprinkled it with sacrificial (*haviṣya*) substances, they should give it in this manner; whatever they give, that indeed they should sprinkle with sacrificial substances. "Sacrificial" is a designation for sesame seeds. [The rule for] cleaning the teeth follows.

Having brought water for bathing and water for washing the feet, he first seats three pure Brahmins. He says: "May my fathers come to their portion from the oceanic waters, summoned by Virāj; live upon this imperishable [offering] which has been presented by me; rejoice in it with the *svadhā* call. Then, having prepared the *viṣṭara* (seating grass) mats from *darbha* grass cut near the roots and arranged in a counter-clockwise direction (*prasavya*), he proceeds.

One should offer [the seat] to the Brahmins, saying: "This is the seat for you, O Father; and for those who follow you here, this is the seat. In the same way for the grandfather and the great-grandfather. One should offer water for the oblation through a strainer, as well as perfumes and flowers. Having taken a portion of the food and sprinkled it with clarified butter, and having taken the darbha grass for the surrounding strew, one should ask the Brahmins for permission, saying: "I shall perform the offering in the fire."
Having first carried forward the fire facing south, shaking it three times while moving clockwise, he strews grass around the fire;

wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he sprinkles water three times counter-clockwise and three times clockwise, wearing the cord over the right shoulder and three times counter-clockwise. The fuel consists of udumbara wood, as do the enclosing sticks and the stirring-spoon; having prepared the strainer and purified the food, he throws the strainer into the fire and [stirs] with the spoon.

Having become invested with the sacrificial cord (*yajñopavītī*), he offers oblations, saying: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! To Soma Pitṛmat, *svadhā*, obeisance, *svāhā*! Then, having touched water, he says: "To Yama Aṅgirasvat, *svāhā*! and throws the stirring-ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) after the first [oblation]. Having performed prostrations, he should sprinkle water three times around [the fire] to the right according to the respective deity; then, being invested with the cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he sprinkles it three times counter-clockwise.
Having increased the food along with its condiments in the vessels, he pours milk or ghee over them while they are still raw, saying: "The raw has been made cooked;

the nectar (amṛta) has entered; what was offered by me, rejoice in it with the *svadhā* call. He then points to the increased portions, saying: "O fathers, this is your portion, the nectar placed in the vessels, accompanied by *svadhā*."
Live upon this which does not diminish; rejoice in the *svadhā* offered by me.
Immortal indeed is speech; O Agni, you are the immortal of speech, the threefold one with a single abode.
Rejoice here with these offerings presented by me according to the *svadhā* offering; may there be greater wealth for us, O gods.
This is the supreme sacrifice for the ancestors, O Agni: that which is to be given to worthy recipients, having the ancestors as its deity.
O ancestors, may our speech and mind perceive these offerings; partake with delight in the *svadhā* offered by the Aśvins.
Those Fathers who are here on earth, those who are in the intermediate space, and those who dwell in the ocean;
or those who, having attained Speech, became immortal—may they all rejoice in this oblation.
This is your vigor, this is your *svadhā*; eat and drink, and let it not fail you.
Carry forth the *svadhā* to the womb of immortality; O Fathers, partake of that *svadhā* which is here.

"O Fathers, you whose deity is *ūrj* (nourishment), may we live for a hundred autumns through her; grant me a luminous and undecaying lifespan. Then, having set these [foods] aside for the Brahmins, he touches them with his own thumb, saying, "Svadhā to such-and-such, svadhā to such-and-such," and while they are eating, he consecrates them with the mantra: "Whatever of mine was not desired... and so on. "And whatever of mine was not desired... and so forth.
Or let it be as much as desired, whether poured into a Brāhmaṇa or a non-Brāhmaṇa.

Whatever has spilled, may the fierce Vāta [wind] purify that which causes our fathers and the deities to be pleased. May Vāyu purify all of that; with that which is purified, may the deities rejoice; in that which is purified, may the fathers rejoice—thus he stepped across the ocean.

Having thus sung the *āśva* hymn and asked whether it has been successfully completed, he, having become invested with the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*), should offer water for sipping (*ācamayet*). Having said, "May you be delighted," and having circumambulated [the guests] from left to right, he follows them as they depart while reciting the mantra: "Whatever [impurity] a woman, a bird, or a beast of prey, or whatever impure thing has consumed of that which was prepared by mantra..."
"May Vaiśvānara Savitṛ purify that; may the deities rejoice in that which has been purified; may the ancestors rejoice in that which has been purified. (JaimGS 2.1)
Having obtained permission regarding the remnants and having returned, he should smear a square area extending eastward from the south with cow-dung; then,

having drawn a line in the middle with a wooden stick while reciting, "Struck away are the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the Piśācas who sit among the Pitṛs," [he addresses] those who assume various forms...

"Being Asuras, they move about by means of their own nature; those who carry away the *parāpur* and *nipura*, may Agni drive them away from this world"—saying this, he places a firebrand to the south.

Having strewn *darbha* grass along the line of the furrow, he causes [the ancestors] to sip water with a vessel of water, saying: "Sip water, O Father, N.N., and those who follow you here; let them also sip.
In the same way for the grandfather, and in the same way for the great-grandfather. Upon these [spots], he places the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) with his open hand, saying: "This for you, N.N."
"O Fathers, and those who follow you here, to them [be] *svadhā* and obeisance (*namaḥ*). In this same way, he offers to the grandfather and the great-grandfather.
For one who does not know their names, he says: "O Father, this is for you; O Grandfather, this is for you; O Great-grandfather, this is for you. For one who knows their kinship, he says:
"This is for the fathers dwelling on earth; this is for the grandfathers dwelling in the intermediate space; this is for the great-grandfathers [dwelling in heaven]."

At the verse "To those who have gone to heaven," [he says] "O Fathers, rejoice; drink according to your portions. Having turned toward the north and remained there until the water has ceased to drip, he mutters, "The Fathers have rejoiced; they have drunk according to their portions. Having caused them to sip water as before, having loosened his girdle, and having performed prostrations, he assigns the garments according to the respective deities with the formula, "This below for the Fathers," where "this below" refers to wool, a tuft of wool, a fringe, or a garment.

"O Fathers, [give us] clothing; O Fathers, [give us] houses; O Fathers, bestow upon us a child, a boy adorned with a lotus-garland, so that there may be a man here"—with these words he gives collyrium and ointment.

Saying "May he anoint himself, O So-and-so," and "May he anoint himself, O So-and-so," he should offer perfumes and flowers. He worships with the six salutations beginning with "Homage to you, O Fathers," and "Homage to you, O Fathers, [grant] mind to us."

"O Fathers, homage to you for your vigor; O Fathers, homage to you for your life; O Fathers, homage to you for your dread; O Fathers, homage to you for your strength; O Fathers, homage to you for your wrath and for the *svadhā* offering—homage to you, O Fathers! Having thus poured out water with the mantra: "Carrying nourishment, immortality, clarified butter, milk, sweet drink, and flowing libation—you are the *svadhā*; satisfy my fathers," he consecrates it with the mantra: "May it not fail me."
May it not perish for me; may my merit be great. May the Brahmins enjoy my food, food upon food.
May this merit of mine, consisting of the water of immortality flowing in a thousand streams, abide in the highest heaven.

"May the gods and the ancestors subsist upon this pūrtam (meritorious gift) of mine here; may they subsist upon it without it ever being exhausted; rejoice in this which has been offered by me with the svadhā-call. Having circumambulated [the site] clockwise with the verse, "Those who are my kin, well-disposed," he should eat the piṇḍas with the verse, "Those who are my kin, well-disposed, living among the living—may their prosperity be established in me in this world for a hundred years. One who is afflicted by disease or one who desires food should eat the piṇḍas.

Or he should consume it in fire or in water; or they should throw it away; or they should make a goat, a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa eat it; then he may eat of the remainder, but he should not reach satiety with food.
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 2.3:

After the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon, there are three dark fortnights; in each of these, there is one Aṣṭakā—namely, the Śākāṣṭakā, the Māṃsāṣṭakā, and the Apūpāṣṭakā. In that [rite], vegetables, meat, and cakes are the oblations, along with boiled rice; for these oblations, [the sacrifice is performed] in the fire according to the procedure for a Sthālīpāka.

He should offer oblations, saying: "To Aṣṭakā, Svāhā! To Ekāṣṭakā, Svāhā! To Aṣṭakā the bounteous, Svāhā! To Saṃvatsara, Parivatsara, Idāvatsara, and Idvatsara—make offerings with their names! Through you, may we long live unslain in the goodwill of those worthy of sacrifice, Svāhā! Having offered thus, he stands near [the cow], saying: "Come, Bhaga! Come, Bhaga! Come, Bhaga! He should cause the middle [cow] to be brought; he should sprinkle it for Aṣṭakā; of that [cow], there are three [parts].
He removes the left [parts]: the rib, the apaghani, and the hip. On the following day, he performs the Anvaṣṭakya Śrāddha, or on that very same day;

having seated the Brāhmaṇas worthy of the sacrificial oblation and having gratified them, he leads six fires from that [central] fire toward the south and causes a pit to be dug for each one of them—one span in length, three finger-breadths deep according to the measurement of the earth, or less by one finger-breadth.
Upon those [straw mats], he places the rice-balls (piṇḍas) while reciting their names. With his hand, he draws away the Mañjas grass for the ancestors.
Some Adhvaryu priests recite that this applies to the sides of the women's [mats]. There, the wife of one desiring offspring should eat the middle rice-ball;
likewise, she should eat the cooked offering (sthālīpāka) of the Śrāddha, or the cooked offering of the Śrāddha. JaimGS_2.3 //
Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra 2.4:
Upon the death of one who has maintained the sacred fires, having procured three hundred and sixty palāśa twigs, he should fashion an image with them;
he should place fifty on the head, ten on the neck, a hundred on the two arms, and [ten] on the fingers.

Furthermore, one should place ten [strokes] on the chest, thirty on the abdomen, and likewise a hundred on the thighs; ten on the penis, thirty on the knees and shanks, and ten on the toes of the feet—it is known that the bodies of a person consist of this many parts. In the center of the body is the *satī*-body, with its hair shaved and nails clipped, thoroughly washed.

They place him upon the funeral pyre here; they collect the sacrificial vessels and place him upon that pyre; one should place two *sruva* ladles in his nostrils—by means of this *anuvāka*, "He who knows thus, when he is suffering," having previously taken four portions of clarified butter and having placed another piece of gold in his mouth as available, and having pushed back the fires, he worships them with Sāman chants, beginning with "The eagle on the vault of heaven" (*nāke suparṇam*), which is to be sung in the village after sunrise.

When the smoke has ascended into the fire with the verse, "O smoke, let this thy smoke rise up," he [should offer] with either of these two [verses], "O Agni, be gracious" or "Thou art great. "The other world is turned away," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
If the wife of one who has established the sacred fires should die first, he should burn her with fire produced by friction or with *sāṃtapana* fire.

Having prepared a burial ground that is not saline, dug out by himself, and where water flows away from the center, and having burned the body there where herbs grow, [he proceeds] for the performance of the water-libation rite.

They proceed without looking back; they do not perform [this] while in the funeral processions (*vāhinī*). Whosoever among them is born later shall take the lead. Having dug a pit near the water at a place where there is no water, he draws up water once with the ring finger of his left hand, pronouncing the name of the deceased. If it is during the processions, having tied up the hair, immersed himself, and offered one handful of water, he should grasp the hair and then take hold of the fire from the torch at the front.

Saying, "O Śūkāha, may you drive away my sin," he should touch a *śamī* tree; saying, "You are a pacifier (*śamī*), pacify my sin," he should touch a stone; saying, "You are a stone, you are firm; may I become firm," he should touch cow dung that has been moistened with water. Sitting facing south, those following him sit down behind him, and he addresses them with auspicious words. At the time of sunset, they enter the village.

They shall remain for that night with a single *māṣa* bean for the sake of peace; on the following day, having mixed milk and water, he sprinkles the remains with the horn of a goat, the horn of a cow, a vessel made of clay, or a hollowed-out gourd. On the third day, having mixed them with fragrant herbs, he should place them in a jar while soothing them with a branch of *śamī* or a branch of *palāśa*. If it is a woman, he should place them in a *vaṭa* tree; then, having passed by a crossroads, [he places them] at a great tree.
Or one should bury [the body] in a river at its fords. On the third day, they bathe the deceased with *apāmārga* grass, earth, and cow dung;
having washed the clothes, they remain in this state for ten nights. On the fourth day, they should resume begging for alms. For him, the *agnaukaraṇa* rite is established;
and as long as they desire, they should subsist on alms. After the ten nights, they should offer the *śrāddha*.
They should give [the offerings] until the completion of the *śrāddha*. Regarding the constellations, there is a restriction for those with a single star: in Maghā, Bharaṇī, and the preceding ones;

not in Rohiṇī, nor in the northern [constellations], nor in the fixed ones (*dhruva*). Having seated the Brahmins worthy of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-arha*) and having gratified them, he should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) as a single unit.
He should not say "and after" (*anviti*). He should satisfy them with all the ritual acts. Having performed the following, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder, he returns.
One should not eat the remainder; having caused the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing, one should eat.

Now, therefore, one desiring the prosperity of his house should commence the *gṛhaśānti* (house-purification rite) during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, either month by month, at each change of the seasons, or every year; having tied together *apāmārga*, *palāśa*, *śirīṣa*, *arka*, *udumbara*, *lasuna*, *dābhadrā*, *amṛtatṛṇa*, and *indravallī* [plants].

Having swept the house, having gathered [the refuse], having sprinkled it with water, having consecrated it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using a handful of *darbha* grass, having scattered white mustard seeds, and having offered the *vāstu-bali*, one should offer oblations to Vāstoṣpati in the center of the site; then one should offer a thousand oblations with the *Sāvitrī* verse. Then, [one should offer] to the southeast, then to the southwest, then to the northeast, then to the northwest, or in the center; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of a cow, a garment, or gold.
Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas and caused them to recite "Auspicious Day," "Well-being," and "Prosperity," one who employs [this rite] in this manner nourishes infinite and great prosperity.
Many sons are born, and no children die in infancy; fire does not burn him, nor do fanged beasts devour him;
neither thieves, nor rivals, nor Rākṣasas, nor even Piśācas cause him harm—even if it be his cattle.

One should sacrifice a thousand oblations while standing in the midst of cattle; by this very same procedure, the case of horses, camels, donkeys, goats, sheep, buffaloes, and elephants, as well as other bipeds and quadrupeds, is explained.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the *Anaśnatsaṃhitā*. He should wear clean clothes or garments of bark; he should desire to eat sacrificial food, water, or fruits. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should fetch these himself, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, to a pure place near water.

Or, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the ritual marks, and having sprinkled it again with water, he kindles the fire, offers the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions,
