Having offered oblations to Sadasaspati and Anumati, sitting on *darbha* grass with the tips pointing either eastward or northward,

holding *darbha* blades in his right hand, he should recite the *vyāhṛtis* and the *Sāvitrī* four times in succession; then, mentally reciting the *Sāma-Sāvitrī*, the *Rājānam Somaṃ*, and both verses beginning with *brahmajajñānam*, he should begin the Veda and study it continuously, remaining silent.

If he should stop in the middle, or if someone else should speak in the middle, or if he should stop in the middle, he should restrain his breath three times, sip water, and begin from the very point where he left off.

If he lacks inspiration, he should study for as long as it takes to master one Veda; whatever he knows—whether from the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda—he shall attain that, its Brāhmaṇa, its phonology, its deity, or its Sāman chant.

Having studied the twelve *saṃhitās*, one attains the world of Prajāpati through them; having studied a thousand *saṃhitās* while fasting, one becomes Brahman, free from passion, and moving at will, attains all desires. One who practices this for a year while subsisting on alms gains sight; for six months subsisting on barley-gruel, for four months subsisting on water and barley-meal, and for two months [subsisting on air].
Subsisting on fruit for a month, or subsisting on water for twelve nights, or fasting entirely, one quickly becomes invisible;
one purifies seven preceding generations and seven future generations, and saves oneself as the fifteenth. This is called the "Divine Ladder";
by means of this, indeed, the gods attained godhood and the seers attained seerhood. Of this very Brahma-sacrifice, there are three kinds...

This [study] begins at the morning pressing, at the midday pressing, or during the Brāhma-portion of the latter part of the night. For this very [study], there are exactly two occasions when study is suspended: when one is personally impure, and when the place is impure. Prajāpati indeed proclaimed this to the Seven Seers;
the Seven Seers to Mahājajñu; Mahājajñu to the Brāhmaṇas—and from the Brāhmaṇas [it has come down].
JaimGS 2.9:

Now we shall explain the guest-offering for the planets (grahāṇām ātithyam), preceded by the ritual of bali-oblations. The planets lead away one who lacks faith, one who performs impure acts, one who does not recite prayers, one who has abandoned auspiciousness, and one who is clearly manifest [in such conduct].
I shall proclaim the guest-offering for the planets— those of radiant activity that move along the path of the constellations— to the abode of Yama; one should perform this rite of pacification.
The Sun and Mars are red; Venus and the Moon are white; both Mercury and Jupiter are known to be yellow;
one should know Saturn to be black, and Rāhu and Ketu likewise.
A wise person should provide flowers of the colors corresponding to the planets.

Having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the ritual marks, and having sprinkled it again with water, he should establish the fire, offer the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) into the embers, and invoke the planets:
Āditya in the center, and Soma, red in color, to the southeast.
One should know that Mercury is in the northeast, Jupiter in the north, Venus in the east, Saturn in the west,
Rāhu in the southwest, and Ketu in the northwest. A circle is for the Sun,
a triangle for Mars, a square for the Moon, an arrowhead-shape for Mercury, and a long rectangle for Jupiter.
A five-pointed [weapon] for Venus, a bow for Saturn, a winnowing basket for Rāhu, and a banner for Ketu; one should know the Lord (Īśvara) as the Sun (Bhāskara), Umā as the Moon (Soma),
Skanda as Mars (Aṅgāraka), and Budha as Nārāyaṇa.

Bṛhaspati himself is Brahmā; Śukra and Śakra likewise [are the presiding deities]. One should know Yama for Śanaiścara; Citragupta is for Ketu—these are the presiding deities (*grahadevatā*) of the planets. Agni, Āpas, Bhūmi, Viṣṇu, Indrāṇī, Prajāpati, Sarpa, and Brahmā—these are the secondary presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatā*). Arka was born in Kaliṅga.
The Moon is in the region of the Yamunā; Mars is in the Vindhya region; Mercury is remembered as being in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa);
Jupiter is in the Sindhu region; and Śakra is in the land of the Ghaṭas.
Śanaiścara belongs to Saurāṣṭra, Rāhu to the Eastern Region, and Ketu to Parvata; these are the origins of the planets for the various regions.
One should offer fuel-sticks of *arka* wood, measuring a span (*prādeśa*) and anointed with clarified butter and other substances, into the fire for Āditya;
for Aṅgāraka, sticks of *khadira*; for Soma, *pālāśa*; for Budha, *apāmārga*; for Bṛhaspati, *aśvattha*; for Śukra, *audumbara*; and for Śanaiścara, *śamī*.

One offers twenty-eight oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning "durvās te rāho" and "kuśāgrāṇi te keto"; with these, one offers into the cooked fire: boiled rice with *ilā* to Āditya; sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) to Aṅgāraka; ghee-mixed milk-rice and milk-rice to Soma; milk-rice to Bṛhaspati; curd-rice to Śukra;
sesame-flour and bean-rice to Budha; meat-rice to Śanaiścara; and variegated rice to Rāhu and Citrarice to Ketu.

With "By truth" for Āditya; with "Agni is the head of heaven" for Aṅgāraka; with "Swell up, let [the waters] come together" for Soma; with "The Brahman was born first" for Budha; with "O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the enemy" for Bṛhaspati; with "According to its ancient splendor" for Śukra;
with "May the goddesses be auspicious for our aid" for Śanaiścara; and with "In what way has the wonderful one appeared for us? for Rāhu’s Ketu.

"One should provide a red goat for Ketu; a red cow for Āditya; a red ox for Aṅgāraka (Mars); a conch for Soma; gold for Budha; a garment for Bṛhaspati; a horse for Śukra; a dark-blue cow for Śanaiścara;
black iron for Rāhu; and an elephant for Ketu. Alternatively, one may give gold for all of them, or whatever else pleases the preceptor."
Just as a machine that has started up is brought to a halt by another machine,
so too does the terrible affliction of those seized by planetary spirits come to peace.

One should not point out a person endowed with asceticism, nor one who has taken refuge in heaven; nor should one point out a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedanta, nor a woman surrounded by her attendants.
For one who is non-violent, self-controlled, seeking the Dharma,
and constantly established in his observances, the planets are always favorably disposed.
The planets, cows, kings, and especially Brahmins—when honored, they honor [the one who honors them]; when treated with contempt, they consume [him] utterly. (JaimGS 2.9)
Thus ends the Jaimini-sūtra.
